primer.text: The earlier notes in this subtopic showed how to turn a balanced equation and a starting mass into the mass of product a reaction could theoretically deliver. This note asks how much of that promised product a real experiment actually delivers, names the reasons real reactions fall short, and gives you the comparison sum chemists use to score the difference.

lessons.title: Actual and Theoretical Yield
lessons.opening: The yield of a reaction is the amount of product you actually obtain. In practice no chemical process ever reaches a complete conversion, because some reactant stays stuck to equipment, some products are lost while being cleaned up, and some reactions run backwards. This lesson names each of those losses and separates what was measured from what was promised.
keyPoints: Yield describes the amount of product obtained from a reaction.
Real reactions never deliver the full predicted amount, for several distinct reasons.
Some reactants stay behind in the equipment and some product is lost during separation, purification and transfer between containers.
In reversible reactions the products keep turning back into reactants, so a high yield is never possible.
Side reactions happen when something extra reacts, such as a gas from the air or an impurity mixed into a reactant.

low.restatement: The actual yield is what the experiment records; the theoretical yield is what perfect conditions would give, worked out from the balanced equation and the reacting masses. Percentage yield puts the two side by side.
low.analogy: Think of a recipe that promises twelve cupcakes: what actually reaches the plate is the actual yield, and the promised dozen is the theoretical yield.
low.examPointer: Only the actual and percentage yields can be measured in the lab; the theoretical yield always comes from arithmetic on the balanced equation.

medium.restatement: Every loss has a name: material wedged in apparatus, reversible products undoing themselves, side reactions eating reactants, and goods spilled while being filtered, distilled or poured. Each one drags the actual yield below the theoretical figure.
medium.analogy: It is like moving house: some belongings never leave the old cupboard, some get damaged on the way, and some you simply drop on the pavement - what arrives is always less than what you packed.
medium.examPointer: If a question lists possible reasons for a low yield, match each reason to its loss point in the process rather than quoting the list blindly.

check.stem: A student records 3.2 g of dry product from an experiment. What is this value called?

options.explanation: The actual yield is the recorded amount of product obtained from the experiment.
The theoretical yield is calculated, never recorded; it belongs to perfect conditions.
Percentage yield is a comparison of two yields and carries no units of mass.
options.misconception: absolute mass mistaken for a comparison

options.explanation: The reacting mass is a starting substance, not the product collected.
options.misconception: product mass mistaken for input mass

check.stem: Which yield is calculated from the balanced equation and the reacting masses?

options.explanation: The theoretical yield assumes complete conversion, so it is worked out from the equation rather than measured.
The actual yield can only be found by doing the experiment and weighing the product.
options.misconception: measured value thought to be derivable

options.explanation: Percentage yield is computed afterwards, from the actual and theoretical yields together.
The balanced equation is exactly what the theoretical yield is built from.

check.stem: A reaction is reversible and no reactant escapes. Why can its yield still never reach 100 percent?

options.text: Products keep turning back into reactants, so the forward reaction never completes
options.explanation: In reversible reactions the products are continually converting back, which caps the yield however careful the technique.

options.text: The equipment absorbs some of the product
options.explanation: Equipment losses can be reduced by careful technique; reversibility caps the yield even with perfect apparatus.
options.misconception: avoidable losses blamed for a fundamental cap

options.text: Side reactions with the air consume product
options.explanation: Side reactions are a separate loss route; the question states the reaction itself runs both ways.
options.misconception: side reactions blamed where reversibility is the cap

options.explanation: Measurement error affects the recorded figure, not the chemical ceiling a reversible reaction imposes.
options.misconception: measurement error confused with chemical ceiling

check.stem: During which stage is product most likely lost when a solution is filtered and then distilled?

options.text: During the separation and purification stages
options.explanation: Filtration and distillation are separation and purification steps, and products can be lost during both.

options.text: While the reactants are being weighed
options.explanation: Nothing has been made yet at the weighing stage, so no product can be lost there.
options.misconception: loss located before any product exists

options.explanation: Transfer losses are real but separate; the named operations are filtration and distillation themselves.
options.misconception: plausible generic loss misapplied to the named steps

options.text: No loss is possible once the reaction ends
options.explanation: Products remain vulnerable after the reaction; cleaning steps are a classic loss point.

check.stem: Why does a chemical company aim for the highest possible percentage yield?

options.text: To increase profits and reduce costs and waste
options.explanation: Higher yields convert more of each batch into sellable product, cutting waste and cost.

options.text: To make the reaction reach completion faster
options.explanation: Percentage yield measures how much is made, not how quickly; speed is a separate concern.

options.text: To raise the theoretical yield of the process
options.explanation: The theoretical yield is fixed by the equation and masses; the company improves how much of it is actually achieved.
options.misconception: target quantity adjusted instead of attainment

options.text: To avoid having to balance the equation
options.explanation: Balancing the equation is still required; yield performance never removes that step.

lessons.title: Calculating Percentage Yield
lessons.opening: Companies compare different routes to the same product, and each route - one reaction pathway - is judged partly on the yield it delivers. The comparison sum is simple: divide the actual yield by the theoretical yield and multiply by one hundred. This lesson runs that sum, then turns it around to catch the classic inversion error.
keyPoints: Percentage yield measures how successful a chemical process is.
Divide the actual yield by the theoretical yield, then multiply by one hundred.
Each method of making a compound is a reaction pathway, built from a sequence of reactions.
A yield above one hundred percent signals an error, usually dividing the theoretical yield by the actual yield.
Yield figures for rival pathways are weighed up before a manufacturing route is chosen.

low.restatement: Take the mass you actually made, divide it by the mass the equation promised, and scale by one hundred. The answer says what fraction of the promise was kept.
low.analogy: It is a scoreboard for chemistry: the theoretical yield is the target score, the actual yield is the final whistle score, and the percentage is how close you came.
low.examPointer: Memorise the equation - examiners expect it unprompted - and sanity-check the answer: any result over one hundred percent means the two numbers were swapped.

medium.restatement: The sum only makes sense when both yields use the same substance and the same units: actual over theoretical, times one hundred. Reversing the division silently inflates every answer above one hundred, which is the tell.
medium.analogy: Compare it to a fuel gauge: put the smaller true amount on top and the reading stays under full; flip it and the gauge absurdly reads over one hundred percent full.
medium.examPointer: Pathway questions often hide the decision: state each route's percentage yield, then name the route with the higher figure as the better manufacturing choice.

check.stem: Which expression gives the percentage yield?

options.text: Actual yield divided by theoretical yield, times one hundred
options.explanation: The comparison always puts the real amount over the promised amount, scaled to one hundred.

options.text: Theoretical yield divided by actual yield, times one hundred
options.explanation: That inverts the comparison; the result would exceed one hundred whenever some product is lost.
The difference shows grams lost but is not the percentage the specification asks for.
Adding the two yields has no meaning; they measure the same quantity under different conditions.

check.stem: A student obtains 1.6 g of copper(II) sulfate crystals; the theoretical yield is 2.0 g. What is the percentage yield?

options.explanation: 1.6 divided by 2.0 is 0.8, and 0.8 times one hundred is 80.
2.0 divided by 1.6 is 1.25, so this answer comes from dividing the larger promised amount by the smaller real one.
The ratio was computed but never scaled by one hundred.
options.misconception: unmultiplied ratio reported as a percentage

options.explanation: 0.8 was scaled wrongly by a factor of ten; one hundred, not ten, is the multiplier.

check.stem: A calculated percentage yield comes out at 140 percent. What does this tell you?

options.text: An error was made, most likely dividing the theoretical yield by the actual yield
options.explanation: No reaction can make more than the equation promises; the classic cause is dividing the promised amount by the real one.
Even complete conversion reaches only one hundred percent; above that the arithmetic is wrong, not the chemistry impressive.

options.text: The actual yield was measured carelessly
options.explanation: A figure above one hundred points at the formula first; no measurement can beat the theoretical ceiling.

options.text: The theoretical yield was too low
options.explanation: The theoretical yield is fixed by the balanced equation; the calculation, not the ceiling, must be redone.
options.misconception: ceiling renegotiated to fit the number

check.stem: A factory can make aspirin by two routes. Route P gives 62 percent yield; route Q gives 78 percent. Which pathway should it choose, and why?

options.text: Route Q, because the higher percentage yield means less material wasted per batch
options.explanation: Yield is a significant factor in choosing between pathways, and the route converting more of its inputs wins on waste and cost.

options.text: Route P, because the smaller figure shows simpler chemistry
options.explanation: A lower yield means more of each batch is lost; simplicity is not what the figure reports.

options.text: Either route, because both yields exceed half
options.explanation: There is no pass mark at fifty percent; the comparison is between the two figures themselves.

options.text: Route P, because its yield is closer to a round number
options.explanation: Roundness carries no chemical meaning; the decision follows the higher yield.

check.stem: Theoretical yield: 5.0 g. Actual yield: 4.2 g. Calculate the percentage yield.

options.explanation: 4.2 divided by 5.0 is 0.84, and scaling by one hundred gives 84 percent.
5.0 divided by 4.2 is about 1.19; the inversion pushes the answer past the impossible ceiling.
The division was done but the one-hundred scaling was skipped.
4.2 plus 5.0 is 9.2; addition never appears in a yield sum.

glossary.definition: The amount of product obtained from a reaction.
The recorded amount of product a real experiment delivers.
The amount perfect practical and chemical conditions would deliver, calculated from the balanced equation and the reacting masses.
The actual yield divided by the theoretical yield, multiplied by one hundred.
A reaction whose products continually turn back into reactants, capping the achievable yield.
An unwanted reaction in which a substance combines with a gas in the air or an impurity, consuming material.
One possible route, made of a sequence of reactions, for manufacturing a required product.

workedExample.prompt: Copper(II) sulfate may be prepared by reacting dilute sulfuric acid with copper(II) oxide. A student prepared 1.6 g of dry copper(II) sulfate crystals. Calculate the percentage yield if the theoretical yield is 2.0 g.
steps: Actual yield of copper(II) sulfate: 1.6 g.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The percentage yield of copper(II) sulfate is 80 percent.
